1. The animation compares fixed yearly raises of 2%, 3%, 3.1% and 6.38% against US inflation (CPI-U). For each raise, it shows how often that raise would have kept up with rising prices. The bars seem to cover historical stretches of time. The 6.38% bar is labeled "Carl's stretch" and is marked illustrative. I'm inferring that the bars measure "kept up with inflation". The image never says so outright.

2. The raise rate changes, and the bars fill in one row at a time. A 2% raise matches inflation in only 2.4% of stretches. A 3% raise matches in 42.4%. A 3.1% raise matches in about half ("half"). A 6.38% raise covers all stretches. The scale runs from "raise a year" on the left to "all stretches" on the right.

3. In US history, a small fixed yearly raise would usually have fallen behind rising prices. Matching inflation in nearly every period would have taken a much larger raise, and 6.38% is the figure shown for the worst stretch. The captions say the data is "US only," "history, not a forecast" and "a median of the past, not an expectation." So the animation is not predicting future inflation.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer might take away that a fixed 2% or 3% annual increase offers limited protection against inflation. For me, that would make the quote's payout options worth comparing on whether and how they adjust for inflation. This is my reading, and it is not a recommendation.

5. The animation did not suggest this advice. It only presents the historical comparison and warns that it isn't a forecast. The advice in point 4 is my own conclusion.
